cite: Gore v. Norwich & New York Transportation Co., 2 Daly (N.Y.) 254
court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: A steamboat carrier that let a passenger a private state-room for extra compensation remained liable, on the analogy of an innkeeper, for a passenger's overcoat stolen from the locked state-room absent negligence, because placing the coat there did not withdraw it from the carrier's custody.

quotes.text: The granting, for compensation, of the use of a state-room, in the absence of notice to the contrary, is a designation of the place in which the passenger may place his ordinary baggage, but not to the exclusion of the carrier, inasmuch as the whole vessel is in the possession and under the control of the carrier, and the animus custodiendi of the passenger, as to wearing apparel in temporary use, ceases when the article is placed in the state-room.
The staterooms on board of the defendant’s boat are similar to the rooms at an inn.
The proprietor of a steamboat is liable for wearing apparel stolen from a passenger’s state-room, in the absence of negligence on the part of the latter.

notes: Tangential to core letting doctrine (holding is about carrier/bailment liability, not the legality of letting), but the court expressly analogizes a paid private state-room to an inn room and treats the innkeeper-guest duties as applicable.

cite: Hexter v. Knox, 39 N.Y. Super. Ct. 109
court: New York Superior Court General Term
holding_summary: Where a landlord's breach of a covenant to complete and deliver a hotel building delayed a hotelkeeper-tenant's possession, the tenant's damages were properly measured by the proven market value of the use of the rooms he was denied—furnished-room value for rooms he had furniture for, unfurnished-room value for the rest—varying with the season, rather than speculative profits.

That rule simply instructed the jury to give the plaintiff that compensation for the loss of the use and occupation of those rooms for which he had furniture, as the evidence showed the use and occupation of such rooms furnished for hotel purposes was worth, and also for those rooms for which he did not have furniture, such compensation as the evidence showed their use and occupation was worth.

The premises were leased by the defendant to the plaintiff for hotel purposes, which contemplates the provision of suitable furniture for the rooms for the use of such persons as the plaintiff in his business as a hotel keeper should let them to.

notes: Underlying litigated arrangement (Knox-Hexter) is a lease of a hotel building; relevant to the corpus because the court recognizes the value of letting furnished hotel rooms as an ordinary, market-provable commercial activity.
